Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

game, wolves, snow, bone/hide/sinew/fat (band stores), glut (household).
- Spreading: PassOn in conversation (both ways), children watching someone work,
  and visits, so ideas cross bands when people meet. Lost when the last knower dies.
- Pacing (design decision for the user): DiscoveryRate 2e-5 gave 89 stages in 40 y
  (bows in year 4); 1.6e-6 gave ~50 different stages on the map in 50 y; set to
  6e-7 so god nudges have room to matter. Runner --discovery overrides, and the
  run summary lists discoveries.

## Social stage 2 (group acts) and stage 3 (between bands), 2026-10-04
  adults they learn from; adult experience (hunger, wounds, kin deaths, talk) moves
  drives away from it and they relax back (~0.3%/day). Culture still accumulates
  across generations; nothing ratchets.
- Teen fertility: conception chance 20% of peak at 16 rising to full by 22
  (forager first births ~19). Tests trimmed (suite 21 min → 3 min).
- State after all five stages (6 worlds × 60 y): map 245-406 people; illness the
  top killer; starvation 14-25%; violence 7-13% of deaths; raids 0-12; couple
  breakups 0-45 per founding band; infants 20-35%, under-15 30-51%; 17-28 stages
  discovered per world and spread between bands. Bands diverge in drives (0.29-0.68),
  sharing (0.31-0.55), peace (0.53-0.75) and how badly they expect a seen take to go.

### Open items
- Land richness final calibration (now 1.0; populations slightly above the
  160-320 target).
- Speed (~4 s per simulated year at ~150 people; spread across systems).
- Hunting methods: ambush (drives are in).
- Discovery pacing is a design decision for the user (DiscoveryRate 6e-7).
- Remaining authored lessons: the sharing/valor/peace "BandLearns" hooks (hard
  AccidentRate 1e-5 per hour out. ChestRisk 0.003, WeaningRisk 4 (fitted).
  PlantDensity 1.3 (now that knowledge is imperfect and loads are limited).
- 30 y, 6 worlds: pop 157-255; starvation 0-6%; violence 0-22% of deaths; killings
  ≤0.07 per band-year; seen takes ≤1 per band-year; splits 0.12-0.16; infants
  21-40%, under-15 30-52%; births ~48/1000 vs deaths 17-35 (still growing).
### Long run (60 y, 6 worlds, richness 1.3)
- No crashes. Violence 0-17% of deaths, starvation 1-6%, killings ≤0.03 per
  band-year, 32-42 different stages discovered per world.
- Populations keep growing ~2.5-3%/yr (≈140 → 300-580): deaths 16-31/1000 vs
  births ~46. Real foragers grew ~0%. Testing richness 1.0 vs 1.3 over 60 y.
### Speed
- Telling places compared every recent sighting against every one the listener
  had (~30k comparisons per conversation). Sightings are now keyed by herd.
  Conversation 24 → 5 µs; a 3-year run 17.3 → 10.7 s.
### Final calibration of the night
- Richness 1.0 vs 1.3 over 60 y: both keep growing (1.0: 290-600; 1.3: 330-830)
  with little starvation. Food isn't the brake; children survived too often
  (under-15 deaths 20-40% vs forager ~45-50%) because well-fed children beat
  infections. Refit: ChestRisk 0.005, WeaningRisk 6 → under-15 37-61% (mean ~46%),
  infants 28-45%; 40-y map 175-288, growth ~1.5%/yr (from ~2.5-3%). Defaults now
  PlantDensity 1.0, ChestRisk 0.005, WeaningRisk 6, AccidentRate 1e-5.

## Open / flagged (not fixed tonight, with reasons)
- Population still grows ~1.5%/yr. Next lever is grounded fertility: nursing
  suppression fading over 4 years may be slightly short (forager birth spacing
  3.5-4 y for surviving children); and births rise after infant deaths (real).
  Worth a dedicated demography pass with life tables rather than more knob-turning.
- Breakups ~0.01-0.05 per band-year (forager divorce is commoner). Needs
  occasions beyond attraction: provisioning failures, childlessness, conflict.
  Left for the next social pass to avoid re-creating the flip-flop loop.
- Violence share runs high (15-40%) in a few worlds mainly because total deaths
  are low; killings per band-year are within target. Will settle with demography.
- Wolves attack on a 25%/day roll when conditions hold (animal behavior; fine for

- Remaining global weights inside formulas (audit G): many reduced or routed
  through drives/learned values; the rest documented as authored structure.
- Belief-layer stages (ochre hand/paint/figure, pit firing, lamps) wait for the
  god/religion work; stepping-stone stages have no direct effect by design.
- Speed: ~3.5 s per simulated year at ~200 people on one core; 12 parallel runs
  slow each other. Decisions (~2.3 µs) and daily upkeep are the main costs now.
- Hunting returns with thrusting spears and real tracking: ~0.09 rations/hour

content.text:
The runs are still going: 6 worlds, about 20 seconds per simulated year each. I'll finish the audit when they're done. Here's what I've found so far.

**What the land can feed:** Running every cell's regrowth across the map gives these maximums, before anyone walks or carries anything:

| Season | Plants (rations/day) |
|---|---|
| Spring | ~1,500 |
| Summer | ~5,600 |
| Autumn | ~9,000 |
| Winter | ~850 |

On top of that, game adds about 150 rations a day and resident fish about 11. An average person eats about 0.75 rations a day. Winter is the bottleneck, so the land's theoretical ceiling is about 1,300 people. Since people can only reach part of the land, the realistic ceiling is roughly 400–650.

Real temperate foragers lived at about 0.05–0.3 people per km². On this 1,600 km² map that's 80–480 people. So the land's ceiling sits at the high end of real, but not crazy.

That supports your point. Starting small and growing is fine; what matters is whether growth levels off at that ceiling. Earlier 60-year runs reached 290–600 and were still climbing. The 120-year runs will show whether hunger ever starts holding the population in check.

content.text:
The 6 test worlds are 72–88 years into the 120-year runs. The full life tables only print when they finish, but the yearly population totals already show the main problem.

**Population over time:**

| World | Y10 | Y30 | Y50 | Y70 | Y80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 123 | 186 | 295 | 506 | — |
| 2 | 113 | 197 | 328 | 604 | — |
| 3 | 121 | 155 | 262 | 378 | 445 |
| 4 | 139 | 231 | 359 | 598 | — |
| 5 | 91 | 150 | 268 | 431 | 565 |
| 6 | 117 | 135 | 208 | 354 | 473 |

Growth doesn't level off. It speeds up instead: about 1.5% a year early on, 2.5–3.5% a year after year 50. Every world has already passed the 400–650 ceiling I estimated for the land, and passed 480, the top of what real foragers would number on a map this size.

So you're right that the problem isn't growth itself, it's the missing ceiling. Nothing slows growth as the land fills up. Three likely reasons, which I'll confirm or rule out when the tables finish:

1. **New bands claim fresh land for free.** Bands split and set up camp in empty country, so each band stays small and well fed in its own patch. The map-wide total can climb until the whole map is full, and the map can feed more than I estimated because nobody is competing yet.
2. **Hunger doesn't kick in early enough.** Women's fertility only drops when they get thin (fertility is scaled by how well fed they are, cubed). So births stay at full rate until people are actually starving. Real foragers felt crowding much earlier: longer walks to food, more work, slightly lower fertility and more disease well before outright hunger.
3. **Winter may be too easy.** Body fat carries people through several lean weeks, and hunting fills the gap, so the lean season never thins the population much.

**Still to come** when the runs finish (probably another 30–60 minutes, since bigger worlds run slower):
- death rates by age, and how long people live;
- births per woman, spacing between babies, and age at first birth;
- causes of death by age;
- how many people are paired, and how often couples break up.

Those will show whether the excess is too many births or too few adult deaths. That split decides the fix, and I'll bring both to you before changing anything.

I've also gone through the code for the other flags. Breakups are still too rare because the only reason anyone leaves is falling for someone free. Discovery pacing is your call. The wolf attack check is the 25%-a-day dice roll. I'll go through all of them alongside the demography results.

content.text:
You're right about reason 1. Bands splitting off into empty land is how humans actually spread, so the sim doing it is correct. It also changes what I should be testing. Splitting doesn't need to be stopped. The test is what happens once the empty land runs out.

**What I meant by "no competition yet":** while bands are few and far apart, their foraging areas don't overlap. Each band is picking its own untouched patch, so there's nothing to compete over. That's real too: a growing population on an empty continent isn't held back by anything.

**How competition should work.** It should come from two structural sources, with no "territory" rule written in:

1. **Shared food running out.** This is mostly there already. Plants, fish and game are shared: if a neighbouring band strips a hillside of berries, there are fewer for you, and the herds are the same herds. Once foraging areas start to overlap, people should automatically face longer walks, emptier patches, thinner bodies, fewer conceptions and more deaths from disease. Growth should then level off by itself.
2. **Run-ins with other bands.** Meeting other people on shared ground already exists, as encounters, grudges and raids, and people already treat ground near enemies as risky. Territory can grow out of that: if a band keeps having bad meetings in some valley, its people learn to stay out of it. That's how real forager territories formed, as learned and defended habits rather than drawn borders.

**Why it might not be working.** The populations are already past where the land should start pushing back, and growth is speeding up rather than slowing. So something in source 1 isn't working. Things I'll check before claiming anything:
- **Off-map game.** The ecology keeps a region-wide pool for each animal. If it keeps restocking the map with herds from off the edge, there's free food that never runs out. If so, that's a hidden source of food from outside the map, and it breaks the closed-world rule.
- **The ceiling is just higher than my estimate.** My 400–650 was a rough calculation and could be well off. If so, the map should still fill and level off later, and the real question becomes whether that ceiling matches real forager density.
- **How far apart bands camp.** If new camps always find gaps between existing ones, foraging areas never overlap enough to bite until the very end.

When the runs finish, I'll look at how much food each person gets and how fed people are year by year. If people stay full while the population climbs past 600, food isn't the brake, and the next step is to find where the extra food is coming from. I'll tell you what I find before changing anything.

content.text:
We didn't lose everything, but we did lose the most detailed part.

**What happened.** Background jobs I start get killed after 2 hours; that's a hard limit on my tools. My analysis program only printed its tables at the very end, so when the runs were stopped those were lost. That part is my fault. What survived is the year-by-year population of all 6 worlds, which is the main finding: none of them levelled off, even at 800–1,150 people. What we lost is the detail: death rates by age, births per woman, birth spacing and pairing. The new version writes results as it goes, so a kill can't wipe it out again.

**Is 60 years enough?** It depends on which question:
- **For the life tables, yes.** Death and birth rates by age don't need a big population, just enough person-years. The current runs are already at years 41–52, so those tables will be ready in a few minutes.
- **For the carrying-capacity question, no.** You're right. We need to see what happens once the map fills up, which takes 120+ years and 1,000+ people. Two fixes:
  1. Launch those runs as separate processes on your laptop, outside my tool's 2-hour limit, writing results as they go so nothing is lost. 2–3 worlds instead of 6, so they don't fight over the machine.
  2. Or start a world already near full. That answers "does it level off?" without spending 100 simulated years filling the map first.

**Why it's slow.**
- **Big populations cost more than their size suggests.** The current runs managed about 50 years in roughly 15 minutes while small. At 200 people it's about 3.5 s per simulated year. At 1,000 people it's well over 20 s, because each person makes a decision every simulated hour, which is 8,760 decisions a year. Conversation and gossip grow with band size. Meetings between bands grow with the number of bands squared.
- **6 runs at once share one machine.** Your laptop has 24 cores, but heat and memory bandwidth slow each run down when they all go flat out. That's the fan noise.

Speeding up large populations is already on the flagged list, and it now matters more. If the map really should hold several hundred people, every long run pays this cost.

My plan: let these 60-year runs finish for the life tables, then launch 2–3 detached 150-year runs that write results as they go, so the levelling-off question gets a real answer.

content.text:
The audit is done. First, your hardware question.

**No, I wasn't using the laptop properly.** Each world runs on a single thread, so 6 worlds used at most 6 of your 24 threads, about 25% of the CPU. When you took the screenshot, 5 had already finished, which is why it showed one process at 4%. The fans were mostly heat from those few busy cores, not real load. Two ways to use it properly:
- **Run more worlds at once.** Easy, and helps immediately for testing.
- **Run a world's bands in parallel.** A real engineering job, because bands share land and animals and results have to stay repeatable.

Your laptop has Intel integrated graphics, and a GPU wouldn't help this kind of branchy, per-person logic anyway.

## Demography audit (6 worlds, 60 years, rates from years 30–60)

| Measure | Sim | Real foragers (Hadza / !Kung / Ache) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Births per woman | 5.9–7.5 | 4.5–6.2 | high |
| Age at first birth | 18.7–19.5 | ~19 | ✅ |
| Years between births (previous child alive) | 3.6–3.9 | 3.5–4 | ✅ |
| Infant deaths | 10–28% | 15–25% | ✅/low in 2 worlds |
| Reaching 15 | 62–80% | 55–65% | too many survive |
| Further years expected at 15 | 34–46 | ~37–40 | ✅ roughly |
| Average fed level, every year | **0.99** | lean seasons bite | ❌ |
| Food brought in vs needed | **1.25–1.6×** | ~1× | ❌ |
| Falls and drowning, share of deaths | **~30%** | 5–10% | ❌ |
| Breakups per world over 60 years | 14–34, almost all "left for someone else" | far more | low |
| Violence share of deaths | 19% in one world, ~0–1% in the others | 0–30%, varies | fine |
| Deaths from wolves | 0 | rare | fine |
| People per km² at year 60 | 0.17–0.29, still growing ~2.5%/yr | 0.05–0.3, flat | ❌ no ceiling |

## What it means

**1. Food never runs short. This is the root problem.** People average 0.99 fed in every year of every world, and bands bring in 25–60% more food than they need. Hunting alone covers about 100% of everyone's needs once bands learn it (by years 20–40). That's far too much: earlier, hunting gave only about 0.09 rations an hour. Two suspects:
- the off-map herds restocking the map every year;
- hunting tactics and weapons having become very effective.

Because nobody is ever thin, two other problems follow without needing their own fix:
- **Births stay at maximum.** Fertility scales with how well fed a woman is, cubed, and at 0.99 fed that factor never drops.
- **Too many children survive.** Well-fed children beat infections.

So high births and high child survival are symptoms. Once food runs short when bands crowd, both should come down, along with the population, without any extra fix. Tuning them directly would hide the real problem.

**2. Falls kill about 30% of everyone, which is a clear bug.** About 50 per world in 30 years, including children aged 5–14. The accident rate was set when people spent fewer hours out on the land. Long searching hunts and more trips out multiplied the exposure. Also, adults almost never die of illness, which is the main adult killer among real foragers.

**3. Breakups are too rare.** Almost all of them are someone leaving for a new partner. Couples nearly never just part. Same diagnosis as before: there need to be more reasons to leave, such as a partner who doesn't provide, no children, or a long-running feud.

**4. Violence: you were right.** It's one violent world and five peaceful ones, which looks like real variation, not a problem.

**5. Wolves are irrelevant to the numbers.** They caused zero deaths. The daily dice roll for attacks still deserves to become a real decision by the pack, but it isn't urgent.

**6. Discovery pacing is your call.** Currently about 32–42 different discoveries per world in 60 years. Do you want that faster, slower, or as is? Setting it slow leaves the god layer room to matter.

## Proposed fix order (no code changed yet)

1. **Work out where the extra food comes from.** Measure the off-map herd restocking and hunting returns per hour by tactic and weapon, then fix whatever isn't grounded in real data. Then run long enough to watch the map fill and confirm growth levels off near real densities.
2. **Accidents.** Tie them to real exposure: hours actually spent out, with how risky each activity is, so the rate can't drift as habits change.
3. **Re-check births and child survival** after 1. Only tune them if they're still off.
4. **More reasons for couples to part.**
5. **Wolf packs deciding whether to attack**, and your call on discovery pacing.
6. **Speed:** run worlds in parallel properly, and parallelise bands.

content.text:
Speed comes right after the food fix. The worlds are at years 36–56 now. With 12 running at once the CPU sits around 58%, so we're finally using the laptop for testing.

**Why each world is slow:**
- **Everyone is updated every simulated hour,** 8,760 times a year, even while asleep or partway through a long walk.
- **Some costs grow faster than the population.** Conversations within a band, meetings between every pair of bands, and lookups like "is this person in camp?" that scan a whole list. That's why 200 people runs at ~3.5 s a year but 1,000 is far slower than 5×.
- **A whole world runs on one core.** Only plant regrowth is spread across cores.

**What I'd do, in order:**
1. **Profile at ~1,000 people.** Find what actually dominates at big sizes rather than guessing.
2. **Cheap fixes first.** Swap list scans for fast lookups (who's in camp, finding a nursing mother) and cut the throwaway temporary objects the hottest code creates every hour. Probably 1.5–3×, with no change to the sim's behaviour.
3. **Skip idle hours.** Someone sleeping or partway through a 6-hour walk doesn't need checking every hour; only wake them when something could change their mind. Possibly the biggest win, but it touches a lot of code, so results need re-checking afterwards.
4. **Bands in parallel.** Bands mostly act on their own, but they share land, animals and meetings. That needs care to keep runs repeatable: same seed, same history. That's the way to use all 24 threads on a single world, and the biggest engineering job here.

**Why food first:** the food fix should bring populations back to real densities. That makes every run cheaper by itself, and it means we profile the sizes the game will actually run at. Speeding up first would partly be speeding up an unrealistic 1,000-person world.

The food runs should finish in about 10–15 minutes. Then I'll bring you the food findings and a proposed fix, and do speed next unless you'd rather swap the order.

content.text:
The food audit is done: 12 worlds, 60 years each. The excess is real, and it's clear where it comes from.

## What the numbers show

**1. Returns per hour are realistic.** My worry about stacked nut bonuses didn't show up in practice.

| Activity | Sim (rations/hour) | ≈ kcal/hour | Real foragers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Foraging | 0.4–0.6 | 1,000–1,500 | 1,000–3,000 ✅ |
| Hunting and trapping | ~0.33 | ~800 | 500–1,500 ✅ |
| Fishing | 0.35–0.5 | 900–1,250 | ✅ |
| Hours an adult spends getting food per day | 4–6.5 | | ~4–6 ✅ |

The stacking of bonuses in the code is real, but gathering is a minor food source late on, so it isn't the cause. Low priority.

**2. Off-map herds are the main leak, confirmed in all 12 worlds.**
- Hunting drove the map's deer from about 2,300 down to 0–500.
- Yet hunters still kill **about 3,000 deer a year.** Almost every one is a fresh arrival from the off-map herd of about 32,000, which barely shrinks.
- The off-map herd regrows about 2,700 a year, which matches the kills almost exactly.
- So the map's people are living off a region 6.7× bigger than their world. Hunting covers 70–110% of everyone's needs, and diets end up about 75% meat.

Without that restocking, the map's own deer are already hunted out, and hunting would collapse.

**3. The body can't feel mild shortage.** How well fed someone is reads a flat 1.0 whenever their fat is above 40% of what they can carry. Even the hungriest 10% read 1.00 in winter. Fertility and fighting off illness both depend on that number, so a plump woman and a lean one look identical. The birth brake only engages near actual starvation. Real women's fertility responds across the whole range: weight lost in a lean season measurably lowers conception.

**4. Food safety: lots of waste, no sickness from it.** 30–90% as much food spoils as gets eaten, because a big kill brings in more meat than people can eat before it rots. Yet almost nobody gets sick from spoiled meat.

**5. Discoveries: their effects are modest, but they all spread everywhere.** Hunting returns per hour barely rose with new weapons. The hunting boom around years 20–40 is people learning that hunting pays, fed by the endless herds. But by year 60, about 40 discoveries are known by about 85% of everyone in every band, essentially the whole map. Bands end up with no technological differences. That's a discovery-pacing and spread question for later.

**6. Why we swung from starvation to plenty.** The old famines were mostly the eating bug, and the buffers added against them were never removed: denser animals, the off-map pool, bigger fat reserves, milk that holds up, starvation only on an empty stomach. Fixing the bug removed the fake famine but left every buffer in place.

## Proposed fixes, in order (nothing changed yet)

1. **Closed world for animals.** The map is the whole region: no breeding reserve off the edge. Herds still migrate between summer and winter ranges, but within the map. Hunting would then really deplete game, and bands would have to switch to plants and fish or move.
2. **Nutrition, which was your idea.** Split food into lean meat, fat and plant food. Real limits:
   - lean meat can only be about 35–40% of what people live on (more is "rabbit starvation");
   - game is lean in late winter;
   - fat comes from marrow and grease, fish and nuts.

   This puts real pressure back on the lean season and makes plants and fish matter. A diet of mostly lean deer would no longer keep people alive. It also opens new grounded discoveries, such as boiling bones for grease.
3. **A body that feels being lean.** Fertility and immune strength respond to fat stores and to whether people are gaining or losing weight, across the whole range, following real research on women's fertility and energy balance. A lean winter then lowers births without anyone starving.
4. **Then run long** (120+ years, many worlds at once, results saved as they go) and check whether the map levels off at real densities. Only after that, re-check births and child survival.
5. **Smaller items:** cap the stacking of foraging bonuses, and add sickness risk from eating spoiled meat.

1 and 3 are fairly contained. 2 is the bigger design change: it touches every food source, every store and eating itself. I'd do 1 → 3 → test → 2. Or 2 first if you'd rather fix the food model before tuning anything. Want me to start, and in which order? Speed comes right after.

content.text:
## 1. Is the map big enough?

**For most animals, yes.** The map is 40 × 40 km.

| Animal | Real range | Fits on the map? |
|---|---|---|
| Red deer | 5–50 km² a year; seasonal moves (valley to hills) of 10–30 km | ✅ |
| Boar, hares, wolves | resident | ✅ |
| Mammoths, and reindeer if we ever add them | hundreds of km | ❌ a 40 km map can't hold a herd's real range |

A real band used about 300–1,000 km², so the map holds a handful of bands' worth of country. That's right for the population sizes we want.

**What's wrong is that the off-map land is empty of people.** Herds really do wander in from outside, but the land outside would have hunters too. The fair version is that animals cross the edge in both directions, and the land beyond is assumed to be hunted as hard as the map is. Then hunting the map out just leaves both sides thin. For mammoths, the pool can stay, but it should be thinned by hunting off the map as well. So I'd revise fix 1: animals move across the edges based on how crowded each side is, and the outside is never a free, unhunted refill.

**Weather is the bigger hole you've found.** There's a random swing in temperature each year (hard winters are colder), but nothing else varies:
- plant yields are identical every year;
- animal birth rates never change;
- there are no failed nut years, droughts, deep-snow winters that kill deer, or poor fish runs.

That matters a lot. Real forager populations weren't held flat by constant mild hunger. They grew in good years and crashed in bad ones, a few times a generation, and the average came out near zero growth. Our worlds never get a bad year, so they only ever grow. Making years vary is grounded and fully emergent: no event scripts, just a random year's conditions feeding into plant and animal growth.

## 2. How real is rabbit starvation?

The core fact is solid:
- the liver can only process about 250–300 g of protein a day, so lean meat can't be more than about 35–40% of what someone lives on;
- explorers and trappers who lived on lean game in late winter got sick and weak while eating plenty;
- archaeologist John Speth's work shows foragers chasing fat, throwing away lean meat in spring, and boiling bones for grease.

**But it's weaker than I made it sound.** A whole deer isn't pure lean: there's marrow, organs, brain, and in autumn real body fat. It only bites:
- in late winter and spring, when animals are thin;
- when there's little fish, nuts or other fat to go with the meat.

So it's a real seasonal pressure, not a constant cap. It's worth doing in a simple form, as a fat share for each kill that depends on season and species, rather than a full nutrition system. It's also not the main cause of the surplus, so it can wait until after 1, 3 and weather.

## 3, 4 and 5

Agreed.

## Revised order

1. **Animals cross the map edge both ways,** with the land outside assumed to be hunted as hard as the map. No free refill.
2. **Variable years:**
   - good and bad mast, berry and grain years;
   - fish runs that vary;
   - hard winters that thin the deer and boar;
   - years tied together, so bad years can come in runs.
3. **A body that feels being lean:** fertility and immune strength respond to fat stores across the whole range.
4. **Long runs:** 120+ years, many worlds at once, results saved as they go. Check whether the population levels off and whether booms and crashes look real.
5. **Fat share of game by season** (the simple rabbit-starvation version), the cap on stacking foraging bonuses, and sickness from spoiled meat.
6. **Speed.**

Should I start on 1–3?

content.text:
## Weather within the map

Yes, that's what drives migration. In the sim, deer move between summer and winter ground on a fixed calendar. In reality they move because conditions differ across the land:
- high ground gets deep snow and greens up late, so deer winter in the valleys and follow the green-up uphill in spring;
- one valley has a dry year while the next is lush, and herds drift toward the better grazing.

The map already has elevation, so this can come out of real causes:
- temperature drops with height (about 6.5 °C per km);
- snow lies deeper on high ground;
- spring arrives later on hills;
- rain varies from region to region, differently each year.

Plants grow according to their local conditions, and animals go where food is good and snow is shallow. Migration then happens because of the land, not a calendar, and people have to follow the herds or switch foods.

## Off-map: open world, no simulated outside hunting

Agreed. Herds coming and going across the edge is how people experienced it. We're not an island.

On your question "shouldn't hunting shrink the herd?" It does shrink: the off-map deer fell from about 39,000 to about 32,000. Then it stops shrinking, because a thinned herd has more food per animal and breeds faster. That's real ecology, and it's why real hunting rarely wiped out common deer. The herd settles where the births match the kills.

So the breeding isn't the problem. These are:
1. **The off-map herd is huge,** 6.7× the map's deer, so it can absorb 3,000 kills a year and barely notice.
2. **The map is refilled every year.** Arrivals top the map back up to its "fair share" of the region's herd, a full restock each spring. Real animals move in from outside much more slowly, mostly young animals spreading out. So in practice the map's people are hunting the whole region.
3. **Migratory animals are huntable all year.** You're right that they shouldn't be. A migrating herd should be on the map for a season and then gone. That's what made real people's lives seasonal: big hunts when the herds pass through, other food the rest of the year.

## Proposed animal changes
- **Resident animals** (boar, hares, wolves, and the deer that don't migrate) live and breed on the map. If you hunt them out, they recover only slowly, as young animals drift in from the edges.
- **Migratory herds** come and go across the edge when conditions draw them: snow, green-up, grazing. They're only on the map for part of the year. The off-map herd breeds without any hunting off the map. How many come through, and when, depends on conditions and on how dangerous the map has proved, which is already partly built.
- **Year-to-year variation:** good and bad mast years, fish runs and winters, layered on top of the differences across the map.

Plus **the body that feels being lean**, which you're on board with.

## Order
1. Weather that varies across the map (temperature with height, snow, green-up, regional rain), with plants responding.
2. Animals move toward conditions: migration emerges, migratory herds are only there part of the year, residents don't get refilled.
3. Years that vary: masts, runs, winters.
4. A body that feels being lean.
5. Long runs across many worlds to check whether the population levels off and booms and busts look real.

Then the smaller items, then speed. I'll check in with results after step 2, since that's the biggest change to how the world behaves. Should I start?

content.text:
## Extinction

Permanent, then. One consequence worth knowing: if the wolves die out, no band can domesticate dogs from then on, because the first dog step needs a wolf pack nearby. That's a nice emergent result.

## Dog domestication

It's there, as four discoveries in a chain:

| Stage | What it represents | What it does in the sim now |
|---|---|---|
| `dog.lurk` | Wolves hanging around camp for scraps (needs wolves within ~5 km) | Wolves are 1.3× more wary of attacking the camp |
| `dog.pup` | A pup raised in camp (needs wolves around and someone interested in animals) | 1.1× more |
| `dog.camp` | Camp dogs, kept over generations | 1.5× more, and the camp is likelier to wake to a night raid |
| `dog.hunt` | Hunting dogs | Hunting skill +0.2 |

**The weakness:** dogs are only knowledge, not animals. A band that "knows" camp dogs keeps them forever without feeding them, and the dogs never breed or die. Real dogs were animals people had to feed, and they could be lost in a famine. A proper version would give each band a dog pack that eats scraps and meat, breeds, guards the camp, helps hunts and carries loads, and dies in hard times. That fits the closed-world ecology we just built. I'd put it on the list after this food pass.

## How much discoveries mattered

So far the evidence says not much, and not in a good way.

1. **Returns per hour barely moved.** In the 12-world food audit, hunting stayed around 0.33 rations an hour and foraging 0.4–0.6 from year 10 to year 60, even as bows, traps, nut processing and drying spread. The hunting boom around years 20–40 came from people learning that hunting pays, on top of the endless off-map herds, not from new weapons.
2. **Everything spread everywhere.** By year 60, about 40 discoveries were known by about 85% of everyone in every band. That leaves no technological differences between bands, and no band having something another lacks, which takes away much of what makes discoveries interesting.
3. **Earlier one-at-a-time tests** (handing a discovery to everyone and comparing):
   - throwing spears cut starvation from 47% to 32% of deaths;
   - cooking and food preservation made little difference to population (about 280 vs 285 people).

   But those were measured back when the eating bug distorted everything.
4. **82 of the 103 stages do something directly in the code.** That's coverage, not impact: many effects are 1.1× or 1.15× multipliers that disappear into the noise.

**My read:** with food unlimited, discoveries couldn't matter. Nobody was short, so a better spear or a drying rack changed nothing. Once food is really limited by closed herds, lean winters, masts and runs, discoveries should start to count, because a band that dries fish or boils bone grease gets through a winter that another band doesn't.

**What I'd do:** once the food changes settle, run proper with-and-without experiments across many worlds:
- discovery on vs off;
- each key discovery handed to every band vs to none.

That measures each one's real effect on survival and population. Separately, look at why ideas spread so fast between bands; it's probably the visits and talk passing on too freely. Both feed your discovery-pacing decision.

The 12-world run with people is still going. I'll bring the food and population results when it finishes, then turn on the leanness change for a comparison run.

metadata:

Balance target for the Anthro god-sim (stated by the user 2026-10-05): without a god, survival should be possible, but societies should *not* be thriving — especially without discoveries. Growth and prosperity should come from discoveries and from the player's (god's) influence.

**Why:** the god layer and the discovery system need room to matter; a world that thrives on its own makes both pointless (this is why the 2026-10-05 food audit treated "everyone fed 0.99 all year, 2-3%/yr growth" as a bug).

**How to apply:** when calibrating food, demography or ecology, aim for marginal baseline worlds (near-zero growth, real lean seasons, occasional band extinctions OK, map-wide extinction rare) and check that discoveries measurably improve survival. Use with-vs-without-discovery runs to verify. Related: [[anthro-design-principles]].

content.text:
The run with all three changes has started; it'll take roughly 30 minutes. Here's what the previous run showed, with only the new ecology and none of the behaviour fixes.

**Ecology only (12 worlds, 60 years):**
- Populations stayed small and roughly flat: 31–180 people, against 300–450 and climbing before. Food is finally the limit.
- There were real hungry periods: a few worlds had 11–16 starvation deaths in a bad year, then recovered. That's the kind of hard but survivable life you described.
- But people **hunted the deer and boar to extinction in about half the worlds** within 30–50 years, killing 10–18 deer per person per year and letting most of it rot. The wolves then starved, and people lived mostly off fish.

**What's in the current run:**
1. The new ecology, as before.
2. The body that feels being lean: fertility drops in lean seasons.
3. The spoilage fix: food is only worth what will be eaten before it spoils. With fresh food at home or meat around camp, people stop going out for more.

What I'm looking for:
- deer and boar persist alongside people;
- populations stay marginal (surviving, not thriving);
- births fall in lean years;
- hunting takes a realistic few animals per person a year.

Balance target for the Anthro god-sim (user, 2026-10-05, refined same day):
- Without a god, humans on the map overall do fine (persist), but don't advance far or fast. Discovery and growth are slow.
- Individual small bands (~30 people) being wiped out is normal and realistic; it's fine if a band the player ignores goes extinct.
- The god's role: speed up innovation/"evolution", drive story/drama and messaging, save people from some disasters, and generally improve their odds of survival.

**Why:** the god layer needs room to matter; a world that thrives and innovates quickly on its own makes the player pointless. The 2026-10-05 food audit treated "everyone fed all year, 2-3%/yr growth, ~40 discoveries everywhere by year 60" as too easy.

**How to apply:** calibrate baseline worlds to near-zero long-run growth with real lean seasons and occasional band extinctions (map-wide extinction should be rare). Keep baseline discovery slow and uneven between bands. Verify with with/without-discovery runs that discoveries measurably help. Related: [[anthro-design-principles]].

## Demography audit and food/ecology rework (2026-10-05, after compaction)
### Balance target (user)
- Without a god, humans on the map persist but advance slowly; single bands of
  ~30 can and do die out. The god speeds innovation, adds story/drama, rescues,
  improves odds. Baseline: near-zero long-run growth, real lean seasons, slow and
  uneven discovery.
### Audit findings (12 worlds x 60 y, scratchpad Demog tool: life tables, food accounting)
- Populations grew 1.5% → 3%/yr with no ceiling (800-1150 people by year 90-107).
- Everyone fed ~1.0 all year; food in 1.25-1.6x need; hunting 70-110% of need.
- Cause 1: off-map "regional pool" 4-8x the map refilled hunted herds every spring
  (map deer hunted to ~0, ~3,000 deer/yr killed from the reservoir).
- Cause 2: buffers added during the "starvation" era (which was mostly the Eat bug)
  were never removed.
- Cause 3: satiety saturates at 1 above 40% fat, so fertility (satiety^3) and
  immunity never felt mild leanness. TFR 5.9-7.5 (real 4.5-6.2); l(15) 0.62-0.80.
- Accidents (falls/drowning) ~30% of deaths (real 5-10%): exposure grew since calibration.
- Per-hour returns are realistic (forage 0.4-0.6, hunt 0.33, fish 0.35-0.5 rations/h).
- Discoveries: ~40 stages known by ~85% of everyone by year 60; per-hour returns
  barely moved. PassOn is one-shot per conversation (8%), so crafts spread like gossip.
### Changes made
- Climate: daily temperature curve (seasonal means unchanged), lapse rate 6.5 C/km
  (authored: elevation unit = 500 m), snow (0.6 cm/freezing day x wetness, 1%/day
  settling, 1.5 cm/degree-day melt; woods hold half), yearly rain districts (6x6
  grid, AR(1)), nut mast (alternating), berry/grain years, fish run strength.
- Cells: local temperature, snow, wetness; plant growth by local warmth and rain;
  foraging under snow limited (SnowAccess). Camp weather = camp cell.
- Ecology rewritten: closed map, no off-map pool. Herds have Condition from local
  forage (authored Need 0.45, dormant forage 0.3, 2%/day); thin animals die;
  births late spring by condition and crowding (1-(N/K)^3); natural death rates
  from field survival (minus predation). Deer migrate within the map (altitudinal);
  mammoths leave the map in winter and return (same animals, unhunted while away).
  Wolves: hunger in weeks, ~4 kg/day, up to 3 chases a day choosing easy prey,
  find prey within ~4 km (authored), pairs disperse to found packs. Extinction is
  permanent (user). Hare meat 2 → 1 ration.
- Body: fecundity from fat (full at 60% of max) and weight trend (Ellison);
  immunity weakens with real undernutrition (fat < 30%).
- Food valuation: food work's base pull scales with room for more (fresh food
  days at home, camp meat vs how long meat keeps: 4 d warm, 20 frozen, 60 cached);
  hunt value subtracts meat already in camp.
### Results so far
- Ecology alone, no people (6 worlds x 50 y): deer 2,000-6,200 fluctuating,
  hares boom/bust, boar track masts, wolves 5-40 (extinct in 1/6).
- Ecology with people (before the valuation fix): pops flat at 31-180; but bands
  killed 1,000-1,800 deer/yr (10-18 per person), wiping out deer/boar in ~half the
  worlds within 30-50 y. Valuation fix aims at this; run in progress.
### Next
- Check overkill fix; accidents exposure; discovery spread (practice-based
  learning, fewer cross-band transfers, slower rate) for the "slow without god"
  target; dogs as real animals (later); breakups; speed.
EOF
echo ok

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.text:
Hunting is fixed. In the last test, 12 worlds over 60 years, **deer, boar and wolves survived alongside people in all 12**. The worst remaining problem is new: lean winters starve too many people. All 12 tests pass, and the full log is in `docs/PROGRESS.md`.

## How hunting was fixed

It took nine rounds of test runs, because there were five separate causes. Each fix uses a real mechanism rather than a tuned number:

1. **Food work no longer looks worth doing when food is piled up.** Extra food is only worth what can be eaten before it spoils, and that now counts all food in camp.
2. **Hunting parties count meat already in camp** when judging whether a kill is worth it.
3. **The meat craving follows diet.** People crave meat when it's been under about 10% of what their family eats, and stop craving it around 40%. Before, the craving was nearly always on, because warm-weather meat rots in four days.
4. **Searching for game takes real time.** A party that finds nothing walks on for hours, so when game is scarce whole days come back empty and people switch to other food.
5. **Hunted herds learn to be shy of people:** heavily hunted animals keep their distance for a year or two.

The no-people test of the land also exposed five problems in the animals themselves, now fixed:
- **Wolf kills overlapped natural deaths.** Wolves mostly take animals that were about to die anyway, but here every kill was extra.
- **Wolves always went for the meatiest prey.** Now they take what they come across, which gives a scarce prey room to recover.
- **Wolves wasted carcasses.** They now stay and feed on one for days.
- **Deer conceived at the wrong time.** Pregnancy is now set by condition at the autumn rut, not by the thin spring condition.
- **Accidents were 4× too common.** Falls and drownings are now about 5% of deaths, as among real foragers.

## Where the worlds stand

| | Sim | Real foragers |
|---|---|---|
| Deer / boar / wolves | 5,000–6,000 / ~2,700 / 29–40, in all 12 worlds | stable |
| People per world at year 60 | 25–193 (one world dwindling) | 80–480 on this map |
| Growth | about 0–1.3% a year | about 0 |
| Infant deaths | 17–33% | 15–25% |
| Reaching age 15 | 41–75% | 55–65% |
| Births per woman | 5.4–7.2 | 4.5–6.2 |
| Accidents | ~5% of deaths | 5–10% |
| **Starvation** | **20–55% of deaths** | a minor cause |

Overall this matches your target: people survive without thriving, and one world fading is fine.

## What still needs your input

**1. Uneven famine (the big one).** Most of the year everyone is fully fed. But in lean winters and springs, the hungriest tenth of people drop to near-empty while the band's average is still 0.75–0.85, and adults in their prime starve along with small children. Real foragers survived lean seasons in four ways:
- **Sharing widely in a crisis.** Here people refuse too readily, or the hungry don't ask.
- **Fallback foods:** inner bark, roots dug under snow, fish through the ice. Here winter plant food is close to zero.
- **Winter stores:** drying and caching. These exist but are probably too weak.
- **Moving camp** to better ground.

I'd investigate which of these is failing before changing anything. Do you want me to start there?

**2. Births are still high** at 5.4–7.2 per woman. It's probably because people are fully fed most of the year, so the new link between leanness and fertility rarely engages. I'd re-check after the famine fix.

**3. Discovery spread.** Ideas pass in one lucky conversation, so crafts spread like gossip. My proposal is that crafts need repeated watching and practice, while hearing about something only makes reinventing it more likely. Combined with slower discovery, that fits your "advance slowly without a god" target.

**Also still open:** couples rarely break up, dogs are knowledge only rather than animals, and speed.

## Famine pass (item 1 of the user's list; 2026-10-05 evening)
User's list, in order: 1 famine, 2 births, 3 discovery spread, 4 breakups,
5 dogs as real animals, 6 speed. (Also noted: band life churns a lot — bad-blood
splits every few years, hundreds of family moves; band sizes 4-26 vs real 25-30.)
### Diagnosis (death logs, ANTHRO_DEBUG_DEATHS / _SEASONS)
- Most starvation deaths were whole camps out of food in late winter/spring, not
  unequal sharing; also lone people in 1-person hearths and orphaned infants.
- Bands shattered into 1-5 person groups: "hard times" splits skipped the
  minimum-group-size check; rejoining only happened when two camps came within 3 km.
- Stores ran out by spring; early-spring land near camp is bare.
### Changes
- Hard-times splits no longer found bands below what members judge viable; the
  family instead joins a known band (anyone in hard times; only the bold strike out).
- SeekCompany (weekly): bands below the size their adults think viable consider
  joining known bands nearby; ConsiderJoining adds a "too small here" pull scaled
  by hardship.
- Demand sharing: givers will share down to the asker's level (SpareFor), not
  only what's beyond 2 days; asking/refusal accounting use the same.
- Inner bark: forest fallback food in winter/spring (~0.2 rations/h × skill),
  only when nothing better at the patch; depletes (20 rations per forest cell,
  regrows 5%/yr) so camps strip the woods near them.
- Births (item 2): Coale-Trussell natural-fertility age schedule after 22
  (0.94/0.86/0.70/0.36/0.05 for 25-29…45-49), fertile to 49; secondary sterility
  (2.5% per birth + complication risk).
### Results
- Starvation share of deaths (years 1-30): ~38% → ~31% (sharing/splits) → ~16%
  (bark). Tiny bands 3-4 per world (from many more); splits now 6-14 people.
- With bark, populations grew ~2%/yr again (100 → 150-200 by year 30) because
  TFR was 6-7; deer hunted out in 1/12. Fertility schedule fix in test (v14).
EOF
echo ok

content.text:
The picture at year 45 in one world: deer were holding at about 5,000 while people took 600–970 a year (about 5 per person). Then a hard winter starved about 1,200 deer, wolves took about 870, people kept hunting, and the herd collapsed.

I've made a lot of changes since your last message, and this has become a design decision rather than a bug. Here's where things stand.

## Item 1, famine: the structural fixes worked
- **Sharing in a crisis:** families with food now share down to the hungry family's level, as foragers' demand sharing does, instead of keeping everything under 2 days' worth.
- **No more microbands:** hard times no longer splinter bands into groups of 2–4. Small groups join bands they know, and splits are now 6–14 people.
- **Inner bark** as a lean-season fallback food. It's slow to gather, and the woods near camp get stripped.
- **Result:** starvation fell from about 38% of deaths to about 15% over the first 30 years.

## The new problem: nothing slows growth until famine and game collapse
With winter survivable, populations grow about 2% a year, reaching 170–350 by year 60. Births per woman are about 6–7, Hadza-like; the real-world fertility curve and secondary sterility I added barely changed that.

The only brakes come late and hard:
- **famine** again, at 25–67% of deaths in years 30–60;
- **deer extinction** in 7 of 12 worlds.

The arithmetic: this map's game can sustainably feed about 110 people eating only meat, or about 220 eating half meat, after the wolves' share. Once people pass that, the deer go. Real foragers at these densities (0.1–0.2 per km²) did live alongside deer. They had more kinds of game (elk, aurochs, beaver, birds) and more fish, and when hunting got poor they ate more plants or moved on, long before the game was gone.

## Options
- **A. Richer real fauna.** Add more species of the right kind for a temperate valley: red and roe deer, aurochs or bison, beaver, waterfowl, and stronger fish runs. More total game, spread across prey with different habits. Grounded, but a bigger job.
- **B. Hunting effort that falls with scarcity.** Hunters currently share every sighting through gossip, so the last herds still get found. Sightings could go stale faster, or tell less. Smaller and more targeted.
- **C. Births responding before famine.** Fertility currently only drops once people are thin. Real women's fertility also falls under steady hard work and long foraging days, which would slow growth before famine hits.
- **D. Accept it.** Bands boom, overshoot, and crash with famine and game loss. That's arguably how many real populations behaved, and it's very much "survive, not thrive". But losing all the deer in more than half of worlds seems too much.

**My recommendation is B + C first** (smaller and grounded), then A later as an ecology upgrade.

Four 150-year worlds are running in the background to show where the ceiling actually ends up; I'll share them when they finish. Which way do you want to go?

content.text:
Taking these in order.

## 1. Splitting
I agree. The point of a size limit is that bigger bands should need better technology. That's how it worked for real foragers: a band of about 25 is roughly what can feed itself within a day's walk of camp, and bigger groups needed things like storage, fish weirs, wild grain, or ways to keep peace among many people.

That isn't what drives splits right now. Most splits are **"bad blood"**: grudges pile up and a band breaks apart every few years whatever its size. In one 20-year run there were 65 splits and 400+ family moves, with bands averaging 10–14 people. So neither the player nor the bands learn "we need technology to grow"; they just churn.

What I'd change, all emergent:
- **Splits come from what size really costs.** As a band grows, the land near camp gets stripped, so people walk farther for less. That pressure builds and pushes a split. Better technology (storage, fishing gear, grain, dogs) raises the size a camp can feed.
- **Big groups mean more friction,** since people know fewer of the others. Shared customs and rituals already ease this in the code. Leadership or ritual discoveries would ease it more, which is the path toward villages and towns.
- **Grudges cause fewer whole-band splits.** Real foragers mostly resolved feuds by one family moving to another band, not by splitting.

## 2. Inner bark
It's real. Scots pine inner bark was ground into famine bread in Finland and Sweden into the 1800s. The Mohawk name for the Adirondack people means "bark eaters". Archaeologists find bark-peeled pines thousands of years old in Scandinavia and British Columbia. But it was a famine food, and you don't have to like it.

It also didn't work out: by getting people through winter, it removed the brake on growth. I'd **take it out**, or at most make it a discovery. That fits your "tech lets bands grow" idea: a band that learns it gets a famine buffer.

## 3. Nobody eats only meat
That was just my arithmetic: the game on this map could feed about 110 people if they ate nothing else. In the runs, hunting supplies about 20–60% of food and plants the rest.

## 4. Hunting: is it a real tracking system?
Mostly, yes:
- Every herd has a **real position** and moves each day by its own choices.
- Each person keeps their **own last-seen sighting** of herds they've personally seen within about 1 km, or heard about.
- A hunt heads to the **believed location** and has to **track** from there. The chance of catching up falls with how far the herd has moved since it was seen, and rises with skill and dogs. Following the trail closes the gap. A party with no sightings now roams and searches.

Its weak spots:
- **Gossip passes exact coordinates.** Sightings spread through camp talk, so everyone knows where every herd was seen in the last 3 days. That's what lets people find the last few herds.
- **There's a small knowledge leak:** a party's list of targets silently drops herds that have died or left the map, so people "know" things they couldn't.
- **Tracks aren't physical.** There are no trails or footprints left on the land, and snow doesn't help with tracking (in reality fresh snow makes it far easier). Tracking is just a dice roll on distance and skill.

A proper version would have herds leave **tracks on the cells they cross**, fading over days, much faster in rain and lasting longer in snow. Hunters would find and follow fresh tracks, and second-hand news would be vaguer ("deer by the north marsh a few days ago"), not exact coordinates. That's real tracking, and it naturally makes scarce game hard to find.

## Proposed order
1. Remove inner bark, or make it a discovery.
2. Rework splitting around what size costs, plus friction among many people, with technology raising the limit.
3. Physical tracks and vaguer sighting news, which should also stop the deer wipeouts.
4. Then re-check famine, births and growth.

Do you want bark removed, or made a discovery?

content.text:
Then I'll bring it back as a true desperation food, set so it can't become a staple:
- **Only when actually short:** only someone whose family is nearly out of food, and who is getting thin, will strip bark. Nobody does it in ordinary times.
- **Poor returns:** about 0.12 rations an hour for an average forager, roughly 300 kcal. That's about half what I had before, since peeling, drying and pounding take most of the effort. A day of it keeps someone alive but doesn't feed a family.
- **Depleting:** about 10 days' worth per patch of woods, regrowing over decades, so the woods near a camp get stripped and it stays a short-term buffer.

That way it might save a few lives in the worst late winters without lifting the ceiling. I'll add it after the current test so we can see its effect separately. The tracking and splitting test is about halfway to the year-20 checkpoint.
